claim: Satellite phones at $3,000 handsets and multi-dollar per-minute calls had too narrow a market, and cheap terrestrial cellular would overtake them.
what_happened: Service launched November 1998 with about 10,000 subscribers against $5bn spent; Chapter 11 on August 13, 1999; assets later sold for about $25m and revived as a niche service.
dismissed_by: Motorola and Iridium management, who projected 30-40m satellite-phone subscribers by 2005
cost_of_error: About $5bn spent on the constellation; $3bn owed to bondholders and banks; shares fell from $70 to about $3.
lesson: A system that takes a decade to build is competing against where the cheap substitute will be at launch, not where it was at conception.

quotes.text: To those who need it, the satellite mobile phone is an absolute godsend, but the problem is there aren't many in that category
quotes.speaker: John Tysoe, telecoms analyst, West LB Panmure

thing: Webvan online grocery delivery with automated warehouses
claim: Thin grocery margins, low repeat use and costly warehouses and trucks meant Webvan's model could not pay for itself.
what_happened: Webvan shut on July 9, 2001, leaving about $830m in losses and 2,000 jobs cut; grocery delivery only worked a decade later on asset-light models (Instacart) and incumbents' stores.
dismissed_by: Benchmark, Sequoia, Goldman Sachs and IPO investors whose November 1999 offering valued it at more than $4.8bn
cost_of_error: About $830m in losses on roughly $800m raised; 2,000 jobs lost.
lesson: Building heavy fixed capacity ahead of proven repeat demand turns a slow adoption curve into bankruptcy, even when the category eventually works.

quotes.text: This is one of the biggest pieces of ridiculousness in the history of the world
quotes.speaker: Robert E. Mittelstaedt Jr., vice dean, Wharton

quotes.text: Demand is weaker than expected
quotes.speaker: Henry Blodget, Merrill Lynch analyst

thing: Juicero $400-$699 WiFi-connected juice press with proprietary produce packs
claim: The press was an over-engineered, unnecessary machine: its packs could be squeezed by hand, and its cost structure was too high for its market.
what_happened: Bloomberg showed on April 19, 2017 that packs could be hand-squeezed; Juicero suspended sales and offered refunds on September 1, 2017 and sought a buyer.
dismissed_by: Juicero's venture investors and founder Doug Evans, who defended the press's QR-code freshness checks and convenience
cost_of_error: Nearly $120m of venture capital raised before shipping; company wound down within five months of the story.
lesson: Ask whether the customer can get the outcome without the machine; if they can, the hardware is a tax, not a product.

quotes.text: Instead, Juicero spent $120M over two years to build a complex supply chain and perfectly engineered product that is too expensive for their target demographic.
quotes.speaker: Ben Einstein, Bolt (hardware VC teardown)

thing: Microsoft Zune portable media player and store
claim: A late, bulkier, DRM-restricted Zune could not dislodge the iPod's five-year lead and ecosystem.
what_happened: Zune peaked near 3% of the US player market, sold about 2m units by 2008 against 163m+ iPods; hardware ended 2011 and the brand was retired in 2012.
dismissed_by: Microsoft (Steve Ballmer, J Allard) and pundits like Computerworld's Mike Elgan who predicted a Windows-style 'perfect storm' against Apple
cost_of_error: Zune holiday sales fell from about $185m (2007) to $85m (2008); Time named it one of the decade's 10 biggest tech launch failures.
lesson: A me-too product with more restrictions than the incumbent cannot buy its way past a mature ecosystem; you need a different definition of the category, not a better copy.

quotes.text: Of course, Zune doesn't really challenge the iPod: it's just a way of establishing a presence in the market, particularly among Xbox users.
quotes.speaker: Guardian Technology blog (Jack Schofield)

quotes.text: Some say Microsoft's restrictions are likely to seriously limit any real impact of the feature
quotes.speaker: The Guardian

thing: Quibi, a paid mobile-only streaming service of 6-10 minute premium episodes
claim: An unshareable, asocial, paid micro-TV app ignores how people actually watch short video on phones (free, social, TikTok/YouTube) and will not find an audience.
what_happened: Launched April 6, 2020; the Wall Street Journal reported the shutdown on October 21, 2020 and the service closed around December 1, 2020; content sold to Roku.
dismissed_by: Founders Jeffrey Katzenberg and Meg Whitman and investors including Disney, Comcast and ViacomCBS who put in $1.75bn before launch
cost_of_error: $1.75bn raised; shut down six months after launch, among the largest startup failures by capital lost.
lesson: Capital and star talent cannot substitute for the distribution mechanics the medium's native winners already use; launch 'with a bang' skips the learning that iteration buys.

quotes.text: It’s unshareable, prescriptive, sluggish, cumbersome and unfriendly. Quibi’s unwillingness to borrow anything from social networks makes the app feel cold and isolated, like watching reality shows in the vacuum of space.
quotes.speaker: Josh Constine

thing: WeWork flexible office subleasing, valued at $47bn privately
claim: WeWork's $47bn valuation was an illusion: a real-estate sublessor with long leases and short-term members, worth at most about $10bn and fragile in a downturn.
what_happened: IPO withdrawn September 17, 2019 and Neumann ousted; SoftBank bailout valued it near $8bn; listed via SPAC in 2021 at about $9bn and filed Chapter 11 in November 2023.
dismissed_by: SoftBank's Masayoshi Son, JPMorgan and Goldman Sachs underwriters, and Adam Neumann
cost_of_error: SoftBank alone put over $10bn into WeWork; value fell from $47bn to bankruptcy with $10-50bn of listed liabilities.
lesson: When the last private round is the only evidence of value and the business borrows short to lend long, price it on its duration mismatch, not on the founder's narrative.

quotes.text: Any equity analyst who endorses this stock above a $10 billion valuation is lying, stupid, or both.
quotes.speaker: Scott Galloway

quotes.text: WeWTF is an especially risky business going into a recession, when the ability to variabilize costs is limited, but revenue decline is unlimited.
quotes.speaker: Scott Galloway

thing: Clubhouse invite-only live social audio app
claim: Clubhouse's surge was lockdown novelty and FOMO; content quality would dilute as it scaled and users would drift once people could go outside.
what_happened: Raised at a $4bn valuation in April 2021 as downloads were already tapering; lost most active users by late 2021, was copied by Twitter Spaces and Spotify, and cut over half its staff in April 2023.
dismissed_by: Andreessen Horowitz, DST Global and Tiger Global, who led the $4bn Series C in April 2021
cost_of_error: Valuation went from $4bn (April 2021) to a 'reset' with 50%+ layoffs in 2023; CNBC: a $4bn valuation that never looked sustainable.
lesson: Growth driven by a temporary condition (lockdown, scarcity, celebrity novelty) should be priced as temporary until retention survives the condition ending.

quotes.text: I think the initial FOMO about getting a Clubhouse invite and trying it out has ebbed away,
quotes.speaker: Matt Navarra, social media analyst

quotes.text: The elitists have left the building. Marc Andreessen isn't doing stuff anymore. The allure of Clubhouse was that you could almost eavesdrop on interesting convos from interesting people. As the interesting people have left, what's the point?
quotes.speaker: Timothy Armoo, CEO of Fanbytes

claim: Viewers will not put on glasses to watch TV at home; with eyestrain, incompatible formats and thin content, 3D TV is a showroom gimmick.
what_happened: After CES 2010 every major maker shipped 3D sets; DirecTV dropped 3D in 2012, ESPN and the BBC in 2013, Vizio stopped in 2014, and Sony and LG, the last two, ended 3D support in January 2017.
dismissed_by: Sony, Panasonic, LG, Samsung and broadcasters (ESPN 3D, DirecTV, Sky) who presented demand as self-evident after Avatar
cost_of_error: Industry-wide R&D, 3D channels and bundled glasses written off within seven years; BBC ended 3D citing 'lack of public appetite'.
lesson: A feature that adds friction to a passive, lean-back habit (wearing something, sitting still) needs overwhelming payoff, and spec-sheet enthusiasm at a trade show is not demand.

quotes.text: Still, if the video display manufacturers are pinning their hopes on the potential success of 3D TV, I’d call for some restraint, at least until the issue of annoying glasses is resolved.
quotes.speaker: Alan Lofft

claim: Always-on face cameras would record bystanders without consent and feed Google's data machine, provoking a social backlash that makes the device unwearable in public.
what_happened: Bars, casinos and cinemas banned Glass, wearers were mocked as 'Glassholes', and Google ended the $1,500 Explorer program in January 2015, retreating to an enterprise edition (ended 2023); but camera glasses returned as Ray-Ban Meta and sold in the millions, so the backlash killed one product, not the category.
dismissed_by: Google and Sergey Brin, who argued new social norms would form during the Explorer program
cost_of_error: Consumer product withdrawn about 21 months after Explorer sales began; Google's lead in smart glasses ceded for a decade.
lesson: A device whose costs fall on bystanders rather than buyers faces a social veto that specs cannot fix; design for the people being looked at, not only the wearer.

quotes.text: The idea that you could inadvertently become part of somebody else's data collection – that could be quite alarming.
quotes.speaker: Oliver Stokes, principal design innovator, PDD

quotes.text: There's a young man wearing Google Glasses at this restaurant, which, until just now, used to be my favourite spot.
quotes.speaker: David Yee, CTO of Editorially

claim: Selling heavy, low-margin pet goods below cost with free shipping, in a crowded field, could not become a profitable business.
what_happened: IPO February 2000 at $11 raised $82.5m; the company announced closure November 7, 2000 and liquidated; the category was later won by Chewy (IPO 2019) on subscription and scale economics.
dismissed_by: Amazon (30.4% owner), Merrill Lynch as lead underwriter, and IPO buyers
cost_of_error: IPO raised $82.5m in February 2000 and the company liquidated nine months later; Q4 1999 loss of $42.4m on $5.2m sales, including $6.4m lost on the merchandise itself.
lesson: Negative gross margin is not a growth strategy; scale multiplies a per-unit loss, so check the unit economics before the brand.

quotes.text: It’s the IPO with fleas,
quotes.speaker: Richard Peterson, analyst, Thomson Financial Securities Data

quotes.text: Wall Street is not a big fan of these e-tail sites,
quotes.speaker: Alan Mak, financial analyst, Argus Research

claim: Magic Leap's demo videos overstated its optics, its core fiber-scanning display could not work, and AR physics ruled out a revolutionary consumer product soon.
what_happened: The Information (Dec 2016) reported the demos were not representative; Magic Leap One shipped in 2018 to disappointment, sold under 6,000 units per Guttag against a 1m first-year pitch, cut about half its staff in 2020 and pivoted to enterprise; valuation fell from $6.4bn (2019) to $450m (2020).
dismissed_by: Google, Alibaba, Andreessen Horowitz and other investors who funded over $2.6bn on private demos; CEO Rony Abovitz
cost_of_error: Over $2.6bn raised by 2020; 93% valuation markdown in six months; about 1,000 layoffs.
lesson: When the core claim is a physics claim, ask a domain engineer to check it with arithmetic before trusting a celebrity investor list; 'lemming financing' is not due diligence.

quotes.text: I knew “the physics” of AR was extremely difficult and I doubted that anyone, even with over a billion dollars was going to solve enough of the problems to have a consumer product anytime soon.
quotes.speaker: Karl Guttag, display engineer, KGOnTech blog

thing: Meta's metaverse bet: Reality Labs VR and Horizon Worlds
claim: Spending $10-15bn a year on an ill-defined metaverse with a ten-year horizon was undisciplined and should be capped at $5bn a year with measurable targets.
what_happened: Horizon Worlds fell below 200,000 monthly users by October 2022; Reality Labs accumulated over $80bn of operating losses by Q1 2026, and Meta laid off about 1,000 Reality Labs staff in January 2026 to shift from VR to AI wearables after Ray-Ban Meta glasses succeeded; the core business absorbed the losses.
dismissed_by: Mark Zuckerberg, who renamed Facebook to Meta in 2021 and kept spending despite shareholder pressure
cost_of_error: Over $80bn in cumulative Reality Labs operating losses since late 2020 (CNBC, April 2026).
lesson: A founder-controlled company can fund a decade-long bet past the point investors would, so the social-VR thesis failed without killing the firm; judge the bet by user retention, not by spend.

quotes.text: In addition, people are confused by what the metaverse even means.
quotes.speaker: Brad Gerstner, Altimeter Capital

quotes.text: As such, we think Meta company should cap its metaverse investments to no more than $5B per year with more discrete targets and measures of success, as opposed to today’s much more ambitious and open-ended strategy.
quotes.speaker: Brad Gerstner, Altimeter Capital

thing: Non-fungible tokens (NFTs) as digital-ownership investment assets
claim: NFTs did not actually secure ownership of the work (they usually point to a mutable URL) and their prices rested on speculation, not use.
what_happened: Trading went from $82m (2020) to about $17-22bn (2021), then collapsed in 2022; a September 2023 dappGambl review found 69,795 of 73,257 collections had a market cap of zero ether.
dismissed_by: Celebrity promoters, marketplaces like OpenSea, and venture investors who pitched NFTs as the base layer of web3 ownership
cost_of_error: About 23 million holders left with worthless collections per dappGambl; less than 1% of collections worth over $6,000 against a $22bn market in 2021.
lesson: When a 'proof of ownership' points to something the issuer can change, the asset is a receipt for a bet; check what the token actually commits to.

quotes.text: Instead of storing the data on-chain, NFTs instead contain a URL that points to the data. What surprised me about the standards was that there’s no hash commitment for the data located at the URL.
quotes.speaker: Moxie Marlinspike, cryptographer and Signal founder
quotes.publication: moxie.org, My first impressions of web3

thing: Facebook Platform third-party apps (quizzes) with access to users' friends' profile data
claim: Default settings let any quiz developer harvest the profiles of a user's friends, and Facebook's rules could not stop developers from sweeping up and selling that data.
what_happened: Aleksandr Kogan's 2013 quiz app used exactly this friends-data access to harvest up to 87 million profiles for Cambridge Analytica, revealed in December 2015 and March 2018; the FTC found Facebook violated its 2012 order by sharing friends' data with app developers.
dismissed_by: Facebook, which kept friends-data access in its platform API until 2014-15 and said its terms of service restricted developers
cost_of_error: FTC $5bn penalty (July 2019), SEC $100m settlement, data on up to 87 million users misused for political targeting.
lesson: A data-access rule enforced only by terms of service is not a control; assume anything an API exposes will eventually be collected and resold.

quotes.text: That means that random developers who ignore the rule could potentially sweep up vast amounts of personal information about you and your friends – and once they've collected it, they could easily sell it, share it, or even turn it over to the government.
quotes.speaker: Chris Conley, ACLU of Northern California

quotes.text: The FTC alleges that Facebook violated the 2012 order by deceiving its users when the company shared the data of users’ Facebook friends with third-party app developers, even when those friends had set more restrictive privacy settings.
quotes.speaker: Federal Trade Commission

thing: New Coke, Coca-Cola's sweeter reformulation replacing the original
claim: Replacing the original formula would alienate loyal drinkers who saw Coke as part of their identity, regardless of blind taste-test wins.
what_happened: Launched April 1985 after favourable blind taste tests; 40,000+ angry calls and letters, protest groups and a lawsuit followed, and the original returned as Coca-Cola Classic on July 11, 1985, 79 days later; by end of 1985 Classic outsold both New Coke and Pepsi.
dismissed_by: CEO Roberto Goizueta and Coca-Cola management, who downplayed hostile focus-group reactions in favour of blind taste-test results
cost_of_error: A 79-day public reversal of the company's flagship product and over 40,000 complaints; the brand recovered and Coca-Cola later argued the episode reattached the public to Coke.
lesson: Blind preference tests measure the product, not the attachment; changing something customers treat as theirs needs to be offered alongside, not instead.

quotes.text: By today's action, Coke had admitted that it's not the real thing.
quotes.speaker: Roger Enrico, PepsiCo North America
quotes.publication: New York Times full-page ad, as quoted on Wikipedia

thing: Google+ social network, Google's challenge to Facebook
claim: Google+ was a knee-jerk copy of Facebook's product that ignored why Facebook won (a platform others build on), so it would not achieve real engagement.
what_happened: Despite forced integration (e.g. YouTube comments in 2013, rolled back in 2015), Google found 90% of consumer sessions lasted under five seconds; it announced the consumer shutdown in October 2018 alongside an API data-exposure bug and closed it on April 2, 2019.
dismissed_by: Google leadership (Larry Page, Vic Gundotra), who pushed Google+ across Google's products and reported large sign-up numbers
cost_of_error: Eight years of investment; API bugs exposed data of up to 52.5 million users; class action settled for $7.5m in 2020.
lesson: Sign-ups produced by bundling and mandates are not engagement; a copy of a winner's surface without its underlying flywheel will be measured in seconds per session.

quotes.text: Google+ is a knee-jerk reaction, a study in short-term thinking, predicated on the incorrect notion that Facebook is successful because they built a great product. But that's not why they are successful.
quotes.speaker: Steve Yegge, Google engineer (internal memo accidentally posted publicly)
quotes.publication: Stevey's Google Platforms Rant (Google+ post, mirrored on GitHub gist)

quotes.text: The consumer version of Google+ currently has low usage and engagement: 90 percent of Google+ user sessions are less than five seconds.
quotes.speaker: Ben Smith, Google Fellow and VP of Engineering
